n: This series of psalms shows a journey from confidence and commitment ({{Psalm 20:1-21:13|Psalms 20–21}}), through anguish and abandonment ({{Psalm 22:1-31|Psalm 22}}), and finally to comfort, insight, and hope ({{Psalm 23:1-24:10|Psalms 23–24}}).
God’s people thank him for giving victory to the king.
God has given the king what he desired. God protected him and blessed him (see {{Psalm 20:5|Psalm 20:5}}; see also {{Psalm 2:8|2:8}}).
The king returned victorious from battle and received honor from the people. His greatest honor came from God, who gave him blessings, life, and his presence.

God offers a rich quality of life ({{Psalm 61:6-7|Psalms 61:6–7}}; {{Psalm 91:14-16|91:14–16}}; {{Psalm 128:4-6|128:4–6}}). This life is characterized by:

- God's presence ({{Psalm 16:11|Psalms 16:11}}; {{Psalm 23:6|23:6}}; {{Psalm 27:4|27:4}}; {{Psalm 36:9|36:9}}),

- joy ({{Psalm 16:11|Psalm 16:11}})

- goodness ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}; {{Psalm 34:14-15|34:14–15}}), and

- protection ({{Psalm 41:2|Psalm 41:2}}; {{Psalm 61:7|61:7}}).
God's eternal blessings also bring a full life now (see {{Psalm 133:1-3|Psalm 133}}).
The king was victorious not because of his strength or goodness, but because God honored his faith.
As long as even a single enemy opposed the king’s authority, God’s kingdom was not fully present. This prayer requests victory over all evil in the world.

The* fiery furnace *and *fire* represent the seriousness of God's judgment on the wicked. In the Old Testament, fire often represents God’s anger against sin and destructive judgment ({{Psalm 11:6|Psalms 11:6}}; {{Psalm 18:8|18:8}}; {{Psalm 50:3|50:3}}; {{Psalm 68:2|68:2}}; {{Psalm 78:21|78:21}}; {{Psalm 79:5|79:5}}; {{Psalm 80:16|80:16}}; {{Psalm 89:46|89:46}}; {{Psalm 97:3|97:3}}; {{Psalm 104:4|104:4}}; {{Psalm 140:10|140:10}}; see {{Isaiah 66:24|Isaiah 66:24}}).

*descendants … offspring*: Evil will end when God destroys all opposition to himself ({{Psalm 109:13|Psalm 109:13}}; compare {{Psalm 18:50|18:50}}; {{Psalm 22:30-31|22:30–31}}; {{Psalm 25:13|25:13}}; {{Psalm 102:28|102:28}}).
*Be exalted* (compare {{Psalm 57:5|Psalm 57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:11|11}}; {{Psalm 108:5|108:5}}) expresses communal praise and joy in God’s greatness and power.
The psalmist feels deeply separated from God (see {{Psalm 10:1|Psalm 10:1}}).
The psalmist switches between thinking about his current difficult situation and remembering the Lord's past faithfulness. He ends the psalm with a prayer for rescue.

Psalm 22 is a cry to God for help. The Israelites understood that the psalm was of David but that they could all use it. Jesus used words from this psalm when he was dying on the cross (Matthew 27:46).

This psalm helped people remember what was true about God. What is true is that God is the King and he does what is right. He has more power and authority than any other ruler. God listens to those who cry to him for help and God saves them.

This psalm helped people talk about what they felt when they were suffering. The speaker felt like God was doing nothing to save him. He felt like God was far away and had deserted him. The speaker described the people who were treating him badly. They were like strong bulls, roaring lions, wild oxen and a pack of dogs. God was the only one who could rescue him from these enemies. The speaker boldly asked God why God hadn’t saved him yet.

This psalm also helped people trust God. The speaker trusted God to rescue him even though it hadn’t happened yet. He was completely sure God would do it. He knew that later he would tell others what God had done for him. This announcement would fill people with hope. It would help others praise, honour and worship God.

All previous laments seem minor compared to this outcry against the enemy and God's abandonment. The psalm has two main sections: 

- the lament ({{Psalm 22:1-21|Psalm 22:1–21}}) and

- praise for redemption ({{Psalm 22:22-31|Psalm 22:22–31}}).

This naturally leads to {{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalm 23}}. 

The apostles saw this psalm as expressing the sufferings of Jesus Christ. He ultimately fulfilled the purpose of David's humiliation, rejection by people, and divine abandonment ({{Matthew 27:35|Matthew 27:35}}, {{Matthew 27:39|39}}, {{Matthew 27:43|43}}, {{Matthew 27:46|46}}; {{Mark 15:34|Mark 15:34}}; {{John 19:23-24|John 19:23–24}}, {{John 19:28|28}}; {{Hebrews 2:12|Hebrews 2:12}}).

- God, the holy King, is set apart from all his creation, but he chooses to reveal himself to Israel. 

- God strongly desires that his people praise him.
Both the Lord and the people reject the psalmist. He clearly describes his pain ({{Psalm 22:1-2|Psalm 22:1–2}}). He lives like a humble animal.

People ridicule the psalmist's trust in the Lord (see {{Psalm 3:2|Psalm 3:2}}; {{Matthew 27:43|Matthew 27:43}}), which shames him ({{Psalm 44:13-14|Psalms 44:13–14}}; {{Psalm 74:10|74:10}}; {{Psalm 89:50|89:50}}; {{Psalm 109:25|109:25}}).
The Lord took care of the psalmist before the psalmist could do anything for himself (see {{Psalm 71:6|Psalm 71:6}}; {{Psalm 139:13|139:13}}).
The psalmist thinks about his past relationship with God (see {{Psalm 22:3-5|Psalm 22:3–5}}). The Lord has been his very life.
Bashan, a region famous for its herds and plants, produced strong bulls ({{Psalm 68:30|Psalm 68:30}}).
The psalmist again shares his deep pain and suffering (see {{Psalm 22:1-2|Psalm 22:1–2}}, {{Psalm 22:6-8|6–8}}). His trouble comes from human beings who act like wild animals.
The psalmist feels like he is *poured out like water*. This describes a temporary and empty life that leaves him drained.

- Facing adversity is as terrible as dying of thirst (see {{Psalm 137:6|Psalm 137:6}}). 

- Jesus might have thought of this verse when he said, “I am thirsty” ({{John 19:28|John 19:28}}).
The wild pack of dogs represents aggressive and dishonest people.

- *I can count all my bones*: The psalmist's enemies have shamed him by taking his clothes. Jesus also faced this humiliation (see {{Matthew 27:35|Matthew 27:35}}). 

- *stare and gloat over me*: Enemies make the psalmist a target of their ridicule (see {{Psalm 35:24|Psalms 35:24}}, {{Psalm 35:26|26}}; {{Psalm 38:16|38:16}}; {{Psalm 55:3|55:3}}; compare {{Psalm 59:10|59:10}}). 

- *cast lots*: Casting lots was sometimes a way for religious people to seek God's guidance ({{Leviticus 16:8|Leviticus 16:8}}; {{Numbers 27:21|Numbers 27:21}}; {{Acts 1:24-26|Acts 1:24–26}}). Here, the lots are thrown as a game of chance. The soldiers threw dice for the clothing of Jesus after the crucifixion ({{Matthew 27:35|Matthew 27:35}}; {{Mark 15:24|Mark 15:24}}; {{Luke 23:34|Luke 23:34}}; {{John 19:24|John 19:24}}).
The psalmist prays to God for help with his troubles. Only the Lord can protect him from dogs, lions, and oxen.
The *sword* shows that the enemy wants to kill.
- *I will proclaim Your name*: The writer of Hebrews applies these words to Jesus ({{Hebrews 2:12|Hebrews 2:12}}).
The psalmist praises the Lord and calls for the godly to join him. He tells of God’s goodness to the needy, including himself.

Unlike how he responds to the wicked (see {{Psalm 21:8-12|Psalm 21:8–12}}), God cares for the needy and listens to their prayers ({{Psalm 51:17|Psalm 51:17}}; {{Psalm 69:33|69:33}}; {{Psalm 102:17|102:17}}).
The *great assembly* might include all nations ({{Psalm 22:27|Psalm 22:27}}; {{Psalm 26:12|26:12}}; {{Psalm 35:18|35:18}}).
The psalmist promises to praise the Lord, the great King of the earth ({{Psalm 22:27-28|Psalm 22:27–28}}), who helps those in need. Only God deserves praise.

God understands what his people need and provides for them ({{Psalm 63:5|Psalm 63:5}}; {{Psalm 81:16|81:16}}; {{Psalm 103:5|103:5}}; {{Psalm 107:9|107:9}}; {{Psalm 132:15|132:15}}; {{Psalm 145:16|145:16}}; {{Psalm 147:14|147:14}}).

*families of the nations*: All clans and tribes of humanity (see {{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}; {{Revelation 5:9-10|Revelation 5:9–10}}) will submit to the Lord ({{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}; see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalms 2}}, {{Psalm 72:1-20|72}}; {{Isaiah 2:2-4|Isaiah 2:2–4}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25-27|1 Corinthians 15:25–27}}).
God alone rules over the whole world ({{Obadiah 21|Obadiah 1:21}}).
The Lord invites everyone, both rich and poor ({{Psalm 22:26|Psalm 22:26}}), to the banquet as long as they worship him.

Future generations will join those from the past in praising the Lord ({{Psalm 22:3-5|Psalm 22:3–5}}). The descendants of the godly will receive blessings ({{Psalm 22:30-31|Psalm 22:30–31}}), unlike the children of the wicked ({{Psalm 21:10|21:10}}).

The Lord's acts of redemption ({{Psalm 40:9|Psalms 40:9}}; {{Psalm 50:6|50:6}}; {{Psalm 71:15|71:15}}, {{Psalm 71:16|16}}, {{Psalm 71:24|24}}; {{Psalm 97:6|97:6}}) show that he is righteous (see {{Psalm 4:1|4:1}}). His righteousness gives him the character needed for leadership, making fair decisions, and building relationships. This virtue brings harmony and order (see {{Psalm 50:6|Psalm 50:6}}).

The Lord promises to care for his children ({{Psalm 34:9-10|Psalm 34:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 51:14|Isaiah 51:14}}). He showed this ability to Israel in the wilderness ({{Deuteronomy 2:7|Deuteronomy 2:7}}) and in the promised land ({{Deuteronomy 8:9|Deuteronomy 8:9}}).
People in the ancient Near East commonly viewed their rulers as shepherds.

Psalm 23 is about trusting in God. It describes God as a shepherd.

Those who pray this psalm are described as sheep. The shepherd guides the sheep and makes sure they have everything that they need.

The sheep face danger. But the shepherd is close to them. He protects them and comforts them.

Many years later Jesus described himself as the good Shepherd (John 10:11).

This psalm also describes other ways God can be trusted to take care of people. He provides good things for them. These things were described like a feast and like being anointed with oil.

Each person’s cup is too small to hold all that God provides. They can enjoy these blessings even while facing danger. Their enemies are nearby but they aren’t chased by these enemies. Instead, God’s goodness and love follow them.

They trust that they will live in God’s house for ever. The house of the Lord was the temple. This was a way to describe how close the speaker was to God.

This psalm, which expresses trust and confidence in the Lord, has been a favorite of God's people for generations. It assures us of God's presence during difficult times. It brings to mind images of the Good Shepherd ({{Psalm 23:1-3|Psalm 23:1–3}}; see {{Ezekiel 34:12|Ezekiel 34:12}}; {{John 10:11|John 10:11}}) and the messianic banquet ({{Psalm 23:5-6|Psalm 23:5–6}}; see {{Isaiah 25:6|Isaiah 25:6}}; {{Revelation 19:9|Revelation 19:9}}).

These psalms develop the importance of: 

- integrity ({{Psalm 25:4-7|Psalms 25:4–7}}, {{Psalm 25:12-14|12–14}}, {{Psalm 25:21|21}}; {{Psalm 26:6|26:6}}, {{Psalm 26:11|11}}; {{Psalm 27:7-12|27:7–12}}),

- God's care as a shepherd ({{Psalm 23:1|Psalms 23:1}}; {{Psalm 28:9|28:9}}),

- God's guidance ({{Psalm 23:2-3|Psalms 23:2–3}}; {{Psalm 25:5|25:5}}; {{Psalm 27:11|27:11}}),

- God's goodness ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalms 23:6}}; {{Psalm 25:7-8|25:7–8}}; {{Psalm 27:13|27:13}}), and

- living in his house ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalms 23:6}}; {{Psalm 26:8|26:8}}; {{Psalm 27:4|27:4}}, {{Psalm 27:8|8}}).

- Sheep rest after they have eaten enough ({{Zephaniah 3:13|Zephaniah 3:13}}; see {{Isaiah 11:7|Isaiah 11:7}}; compare {{Isaiah 13:20|Isaiah 13:20}}; {{Isaiah 27:10|27:10}}). 

- The Lord guides the sheep for their benefit (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalm 5:8}}). 

- Sheep drink only from still water, so the shepherd finds peaceful streams for them.

- Compare {{Psalm 19:7|Psalm 19:7}}; *The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul*.

- The Lord guides by: 

- rescuing his people from evil ({{Psalm 23:4-5|Psalm 23:4–5}}; see {{Psalm 31:3|31:3}}),

- bringing them back to himself ({{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 61:2|61:2}}),

- caring for his people ({{Psalm 48:14|Psalms 48:14}}; {{Psalm 139:10|139:10}}),

- ruling his people ({{Psalm 67:4|Psalm 67:4}}),

- counseling his people ({{Psalm 73:24|Psalm 73:24}}),

- protecting his people ({{Psalm 78:53|Psalms 78:53}}; {{Psalm 107:30|107:30}}; {{Psalm 143:11|143:11}}), and

- instructing them in wisdom ({{Psalm 27:11|Psalm 27:11}}; see {{Proverbs 4:11|Proverbs 4:11}}).

- The Lord’s name guarantees the relationship. He protects his reputation against any claims of abandoning his people or allowing them to sin (see {{Psalm 25:11|Psalms 25:11}}; {{Psalm 31:3|31:3}}; {{Psalm 106:8|106:8}}; {{Psalm 143:11|143:11}}).
The shepherd used his rod and staff to protect against danger.

- A feast shows the Lord’s care and mercy for his people (see {{Psalm 22:26|Psalm 22:26}}, {{Psalm 22:29|29}}). Enemies may watch, but they cannot disturb the guests. 

- The ritual of anointing the head with oil honored guests ({{Psalm 92:9-11|Psalm 92:9–11}}), and provided hospitality and refreshment ({{Psalm 104:15|104:15}}; {{Psalm 133:2|133:2}}).

The Lord shows his unfailing love through his presence and the unique benefits he provides ({{Psalm 69:16|Psalms 69:16}}; {{Psalm 86:17|86:17}}; {{Psalm 109:21|109:21}}; see {{Psalm 18:6|18:6}}; {{Psalm 61:4|61:4}}). He gives care that surpasses the temporary challenges from enemies ({{Psalm 7:1|Psalm 7:1}}).

The Lord made the earth and everything in it, and now he rules over it (see {{1 Corinthians 10:25-26|1 Corinthians 10:25–26}}). He sees all its people ({{Psalm 33:14|Psalm 33:14}}), no matter their status ({{Psalm 49:1-2|49:1–2}}).
The kingdom belongs to the Creator, the Great King (see {{Psalm 22:27|Psalm 22:27}}).
The shepherd from {{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalm 23}}, who is also the King of the world, takes control of Zion.
God created everything in an orderly and stable manner (see {{Psalm 89:11|Psalm 89:11}}; {{Psalm 102:25|102:25}}; {{Psalm 104:5|104:5}}).

- These questions encourage people to stop focusing on their issues with the wicked and to reflect on themselves (see {{Psalm 15:1|Psalm 15:1}}). 

- God's holy place is the holy mountain, referring to both Jerusalem and heaven.
The citizens of the King’s realm include all who seek him. The Lord invites them to enter his presence.

- People with clean hands have not caused harm or damaged relationships (see {{Psalm 9:12|Psalm 9:12}}; {{Psalm 15:2-5|15:2–5}}).

- People with pure hearts dedicate themselves completely to the Lord. This is shown through strong character, honesty, and selflessness ({{Psalm 51:10|Psalm 51:10}}; {{Psalm 73:1|73:1}}; see {{Matthew 5:8|Matthew 5:8}}).
The* LORD of Hosts* rules from his home, the temple in Jerusalem ({{Psalm 84:3-5|Psalm 84:3–5}}). He keeps out sin and sinners ({{Psalm 24:3-6|Psalm 24:326}}) but protects everyone living in Zion.
The psalmist commits himself to the Lord instead of to idols (see {{Psalm 24:3-4|Psalm 24:3–4}}).
The psalmist is confident that the godly will be proven right and his enemies will fail (see {{Psalm 25:15-22|Psalm 25:15–22}}).

This personal lament includes wisdom teachings and a community lament. It starts and ends with a declaration of trust in the Lord ({{Psalm 25:1-3|Psalm 25:1–3}}, {{Psalm 25:15-22|15–22}}). The psalmist prays for guidance ({{Psalm 25:4-7|Psalm 25:4–7}}) and urges the godly to live wisely ({{Psalm 25:12-14|25:12–14}}). 

In addition to the enemies who trouble him, the psalmist confesses his sins({{Psalm 25:7|Psalm 25:7}}, {{Psalm 25:11|11}}, {{Psalm 25:18|18}}) as part of his distress. Trust grows by understanding God's nature: He is compassionate, faithful, and good ({{Psalm 25:8-10|Psalm 25:8–10}}).
Enemies would rejoice by singing a victory song.

The right path, the path of wisdom (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalm 5:8}}), involves being open to instruction that leads to life ({{Psalm 27:11|27:11}}; {{Psalm 43:3|43:3}}; {{Psalm 73:24|73:24}}; {{Psalm 119:12|119:12}}).
In this prayer for guidance, compassion, and forgiveness, the psalmist asks the Lord for wisdom. He admits his past mistakes and recognizes that his hope is in his merciful Savior.
Biblical hope is not just wishing for a good outcome. It means trusting in the Lord's will and having the courage to face disappointments ({{Psalm 33:22|Psalm 33:22}}; {{Psalm 130:5|130:5}}).
The Lord keeps his people close to himself.

The psalmist asks for forgiveness for his many sins ({{Psalm 25:7|Psalms 25:7}}; {{Psalm 32:1-5|32:1–5}}). The sins of Israel’s kings showed the weaknesses in David’s family line and why it failed in Old Testament Israel (see {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}).
Those who fear the Lord will receive further instruction and experience God’s presence ({{Psalm 25:14|Psalm 25:14}}) and blessing ({{Psalm 25:13|25:13}}).

- *prosperity*: See {{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}. 

- *inherit the land*: Unlike the wicked, who will perish ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}), the godly have a secure future. In the end, God will bless them, and their blessings will last (see {{Psalm 37:9|Psalm 37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:11|11}}, {{Psalm 37:22|22}}, {{Psalm 37:29|29}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}; {{Isaiah 57:13|Isaiah 57:13}}; {{Matthew 5:5|Matthew 5:5}}).
*free my feet from the mesh*: See {{Psalm 5:9-10|Psalm 5:9–10}}; {{Psalm 31:4|31:4}}; {{Psalm 140:5|140:5}}; {{Proverbs 3:26|Proverbs 3:26}}.
The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord, commits to a life of integrity, and prays for rescue.

The psalmist finds no relief (see {{Psalm 4:1|Psalms 4:1}}; {{Psalm 13:1-2|13:1–2}}) as his problems worsen. He connects his anguish to sin but does not explain the nature of his sin (see {{Psalm 25:7|Psalm 25:7}}, {{Psalm 25:11|11}}).
The psalmist asks God to handle these enemies, knowing that the Lord hates violent people (see {{Psalm 11:5|Psalm 11:5}}).
The psalm ends with a promise of trust and hope, just as it began (see {{Psalm 9:18|Psalms 9:18}}; {{Psalm 25:5|25:5}}).
The psalmist opens himself to divine examination of his life, especially in the areas of his character and devotion.
In this personal lament, the psalmist prays for redemption because of his innocence and the Lord's justice.
For God’s truth to become part of one’s character requires a habitual commitment.
Because of his devotion to the Lord ({{Psalm 26:1-3|Psalm 26:1–3}}), the psalmist separates himself from evil people (see {{Psalm 1:1|Psalm 1:1}}).

- Ritual purity required the worshiper to wash their hands. This act symbolized separating from evil and evildoers (see {{Psalm 73:13|Psalm 73:13}}). 

- The altar symbolizes God's presence ({{Psalm 43:4|Psalm 43:4}}).
The psalmist demonstrates his loyalty to the Lord through pious rituals, praise, and acknowledgment of the Lord’s presence in the temple.
The sanctuary represented the visible presence of the Lord (see {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}).
*Do not take my soul away with sinners*: The end of the godly cannot be the same as that of the wicked.

- The psalmist standing on solid ground represents salvation (compare {{Psalm 143:10|Psalm 143:10}}). 

- *in the congregations*: This means *in the great assembly* at the temple ({{Psalm 26:6-8|Psalms 26:6–8}}; {{Psalm 22:25|22:25}}).

The psalmist acknowledges the Lord at the center of his life ({{Psalm 27:1|Psalm 27:1}}). Because of God’s presence, he engages his adversaries with confidence. They cannot intimidate him or disrupt his inner peace.

This psalm combines two types—a psalm of confidence ({{Psalm 27:1-6|Psalm 27:1–6}}) and an individual lament ({{Psalm 27:7-14|27:7–14}})—united by the theme of longing for the Lord's presence. The psalmist focuses on the Lord, making his own circumstances less important. The psalmist shows strong faith by being open to the Lord's guidance, timing, and priorities.
The psalmist's enemies want to take advantage of him and live off his resources (see study note on Psalm 14:4).
Seeking and enjoying the Lord's presence gives the psalmist confidence and security. He trusts in God's protection and looks forward to giving thanks and praise (see {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}).
*tent* (or *tabernacle*): This early shrine was where the Israelites worshipped before they built the temple.

- *my head will be held high*: This is a sign of victory. 

- The granting of the request of {{Psalm 27:4|Psalm 27:4}} leads to sacrifices with joyful shouts.

Unlike the wicked ({{Psalm 10:4|Psalm 10:4}}), who only want a temporary advantage ({{Psalm 78:34-36|78:34–36}}), the godly search for the Lord like a thirsty person seeks water in the desert ({{Psalm 63:1|63:1}}; {{Psalm 105:4|105:4}}; {{Psalm 119:2|119:2}}, {{Psalm 119:10|10}}; {{Matthew 6:33|Matthew 6:33}}). They act wisely ({{Psalm 34:10|Psalm 34:10}}, {{Psalm 34:14|14}}) while waiting for the Lord to resolve their crisis ({{Psalm 34:4|34:4}}; {{Psalm 69:6|69:6}}; {{Psalm 77:2|77:2}}; {{Psalm 119:58|119:58}}).
The psalmist asks for the Lord's mercy, presence, and guidance. For the psalmist, God is the greatest good, while enemies and other situations are less important.

The psalmist shows confidence and hope in the Lord's presence. Living in faith means waiting patiently, knowing the Lord is good. This life is not always easy for the faithful ({{Psalm 42:2-3|Psalm 42:2–3}}; {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}), but their future is secure ({{Psalm 37:9|37:9}}; {{Psalm 130:7|130:7}}; see {{Psalm 9:18|9:18}}).
*if You remain silent*: The psalmist asks the Lord to act ({{Psalm 35:22|Psalm 35:22}}; {{Psalm 50:3|50:3}}; {{Psalm 83:1|83:1}}; {{Psalm 109:1|109:1}}).
The psalmist asks the Lord to listen. His urgent request comes from the tension between his close relationship with the Lord and the trouble he is facing.
In this personal lament, the psalmist asks for justice and mercy. He trusts in the Lord's strength and faithfulness and prays for the Lord's people.
People often raised their hands as a sign of devoted prayer ({{Psalm 63:4|Psalms 63:4}}; {{Psalm 134:2|134:2}}).
The psalmist asks God to punish his enemies and prove his innocence.
The wicked do not acknowledge the difference between the sacred and the common, so they have no respect for the Lord’s creation, redemption, or revelation.
The psalmist anticipates rescue because of his confidence in the Lord’s justice.
*my strength and my shield*: The Lord protects the psalmist (see {{Psalm 59:9|Psalm 59:9}}, {{Psalm 59:17|17}}).

- The poem closes with intercession for the Lord’s people. 

- *bless Your inheritance*: See {{Psalm 29:11|Psalms 29:11}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}.

- The psalmist issues a call to honor the Lord for his power (see {{Psalm 96:7-8|Psalm 96:7–8}}). 

- *O heavenly beings*: Angels or deities who, some believed, held special powers. The psalmist did not believe in other gods but called on people who thought they were real to look to the Lord as the only God.
This nature hymn in praise of the Creator declares that the Lord holds all power over nature. God uses the same unsurpassed strength to care for his people.

The Hebrew word *qol* can mean "voice," "noise" ({{1 Kings 1:45|1 Kings 1:45}}), or "thunder" ({{Joel 3:16|Joel 3:16}}). The Lord's voice is awe-inspiring and overpowers any sounds people might attribute to other gods.
The cedars of Lebanon were famous for their large size and high quality (see {{Isaiah 2:13|Isaiah 2:13}}).

- Lebanon’s mountains and Sirion (another name for Mount Hermon) are high mountains to the north of Israel. 

- The Lord can make even huge mountains shake when he commands it (see {{Psalm 114:4|Psalm 114:4}}).
The Wilderness of Kadesh was south of Judah. People could hear God's voice across the land, from the north ({{Psalm 29:6|Psalm 29:6}}) to the south.
The image of strong floodwaters relates to the great flood ({{Genesis 6:17|Genesis 6:17}}). The Lord rules as king over all creation. No one challenges his kingdom.
The ruler of nature blesses his people with peace (see {{Psalm 28:8-9|Psalms 28:8–9}}; {{Psalm 37:11|37:11}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}).

- *I will exalt You* is a call to praise and thank the Lord ({{Psalm 34:3|Psalms 34:3}}; {{Psalm 81:1|81:1}}; {{Psalm 99:5|99:5}}, {{Psalm 99:9|9}}; {{Psalm 107:32|107:32}}; {{Psalm 118:28|118:28}}; {{Psalm 145:1|145:1}}; see {{Exodus 15:1|Exodus 15:1}}; {{Isaiah 25:1|Isaiah 25:1}}). 

- *You have lifted me up*: God saved the psalmist from death ({{Psalm 30:3|Psalm 30:3}}).

- God, in his justice and care, did not let the psalmist’s enemies win (see {{Psalm 26:9|Psalms 26:9}}; {{Psalm 27:12|27:12}}; {{Psalm 28:3|28:3}}; {{Psalm 31:8|31:8}}).
The psalmist praises God for his victory over difficult circumstances, comparing it to being saved from death.

This individual thanksgiving psalm begins by praising the Lord for his salvation ({{Psalm 30:1-3|Psalm 30:1–3}}). It then contrasts God's favor with his anger ({{Psalm 30:4-7|Psalm 30:4–7}}) and ends with a transformation from mourning to dancing ({{Psalm 30:8-12|30:8–12}}).
Perhaps David wrote this psalm before the dedication of the temple, making his own experience representative of the nation’s.
The godly should celebrate the Lord’s acts of rescue with song and praise ({{Psalm 33:21|Psalms 33:21}}; {{Psalm 97:12|97:12}}; {{Psalm 103:1|103:1}}; {{Psalm 105:3|105:3}}; {{Psalm 145:21|145:21}}).

- *I will never be shaken*: The psalmist admits his overconfident attitude (compare {{Psalm 32:3-4|Psalm 32:3–4}}). 

- *my mountain stand strong*: In the psalms, this phrase powerfully symbolizes stability and God's control (see {{Psalm 11:1|Psalms 11:1}}; {{Psalm 18:7|18:7}}; {{Psalm 36:6|36:6}}; {{Psalm 46:2|46:2}}; {{Psalm 72:3|72:3}}; {{Psalm 76:4|76:4}}; {{Psalm 83:14|83:14}}; {{Psalm 97:5|97:5}}; {{Psalm 114:4|114:4}}, {{Psalm 114:6|6}}; {{Psalm 125:2|125:2}}). 

- *I was dismayed*: The absence of God’s favor destroys the security of the proud (compare {{Psalm 104:27-30|Psalm 104:27–30}}).

The psalmist faced death (also in {{Psalm 30:1-3|Psalm 30:1–3}}), either literally or figuratively. When he turned to the Lord, the Lord rescued him and changed his mourning into joyful dancing. Only God's favor can permanently and powerfully overcome human failure and deep despair.
